### Hyperparameter optimization

Each type of agent had a specific set of hyperparameters to be optimized. For all network types, it included the initial learning rate of Adam $η_{0}$ and the initialization hyperparameters $\sigma_{0,x⋅}$, $\sigma_{0,h⋅}$. For the networks without lateral connections specifically, it also included $\mu_{0,h.,ii}$ (for those networks, setting it close to one can help avoid the vanishing gradient problem during training Bengio et al., 1994; Sutskever et al., 2013) for the other networks, this was set to 0. For the heuristic types, it included only the learning rate of the stochastic gradient descent. A unique set of hyperparameter values was determined for each type of agent, each environment, and, for the network types, each number of units, through the optimization described next.

We used Bayesian optimization (Agnihotri and Batra, 2020) with Gaussian processes and the upper confidence bound acquisition function to identify the best hyperparameters for each network architecture, environment, and number of units. During the optimization, combinations of hyperparameter values were iteratively sampled, each evaluated over 10 trials with different random seeds, for a total of 60 iterations (hence, 600 trials) for a given architecture, environment, and number of units. In each trial, one network was created, trained, and its cross-entropy was measured on independent test data. The training and test datasets used for the hyperparameter optimization procedure were not used in any other analyses. The training datasets contained respectively 160 and 400 minibatches of 20 sequences for the unigram and the bigram environment; the test datasets contained 200 sequences for each environment. We selected the combination of hyperparameter values corresponding to the iteration that led to the lowest mean test cross-entropy over the 10 trials. The selected values are listed in Table 1.

For the heuristic types, we used random search from a log uniform distribution in the [10–6, 10–1] range over 80 trials to determine the optimal learning rate of the stochastic gradient descent. This led to selecting the value 3.10–3 for all heuristic types and all three environments.

### Performance analyses

All agents were tested in the environment they were trained in (except for Figure 6—figure supplement 1 which tests cross-environment performance). We used a single test dataset per environment of 1000 sequences independent of the training dataset. The log likelihood L of a given agent was measured from its predictions according to Equation 1. The optimal log likelihood $L_{optimal}$ was measured from the predictions of the optimal solution for the given environment. The chance log likelihood $L_{chance}$ was measured using a constant prediction of 0.5. To facilitate the interpretation of the results, the prediction performance of the agent was expressed as the % of optimal log likelihood, defined as:

$$
\frac{L−L_{chance}}{L_{optimal}−L_{chance}}\times100
$$

To test the statistical significance of a comparison of performance between two types of agents, we used a two-tailed two independent samples t-test with Welch’s correction for unequal variances.

### Analysis of the effective learning rate

The instantaneous effective learning rate of an agent that updates its prediction from $p_{t}$ to $p_{t+1}$ upon receiving observation $x_{t+1}$ is calculated as:

$$
\alpha_{t+1}=\frac{p_{t+1}−p_{t}}{x_{t+1}−p_{t}}\alpha_{t=0}=\frac{p_{0}−0.5}{x_{0}−0.5}
$$

We call it ‘effective learning rate’ because, had the agent been using a delta-rule algorithm, it would be equivalent to the learning rate of the delta-rule (as can be seen by rearranging the above formula into an update equation), and because it can be measured even if the agent uses another algorithm.

### Readout analyses

The readout of a given quantity from the recurrent units of a network consists of a weighted sum of the activation values of each unit. To determine the weights of the readout for a given network, we ran a multiple linear regression using, as input variables, the activation of each recurrent unit at a given time step $h_{i,t}$, and as target variable, the desired quantity calculated at the same time step. The regression was run on a training dataset of 900 sequences of 380 observations each (hence, 342,000 samples).

In the unigram environment, the precision readout was obtained using as desired quantity the log precision of the posterior distribution over the unigram variable calculated by the optimal solution as previously described, that is, $ψ_{t}=−log⁡\sigma_{t}$, where $\sigma_{t}$ is the standard deviation of the posterior distribution over $p_{t+1}^{env}$:

$$
\sigma_{t}=SD[p_{t+1}^{env}|x_{0},...,x_{t}]
$$

In the bigram environment, the readout of the estimate of a given bigram variable was obtained using as desired quantity the log odds of the mean of the posterior distribution over that bigram variable calculated by the optimal solution, and the readout of the precision of that estimate was obtained using the log precision of that same posterior under the above definition of precision.

In Figure 4a, to measure the accuracy of the readout from a given network, we calculated the Pearson correlation between the quantity read from the network and the optimal quantity on a test dataset of 100 sequences (hence, 38,000 samples), independent from any training dataset. To measure the Pearson correlation between the read precision and the subsequent effective learning rate, we used 300 out-of-sample sequences (hence, 114,000 samples). To measure the mutual information between the read precision and the prediction of the network, we also used 300 out-of-sample sequences (114,000 samples).

In Figure 6d, the log odds and log precision were transformed back into mean and standard deviation for visualization purposes.

### Dynamics of network activity in the prediction-precision subspace

In Figure 4b, the network activity (i.e. the population activity of the recurrent units in the network) was projected onto the two-dimensional subspace spanned by the prediction vector and the precision vector. The prediction vector is the vector of the weights from the recurrent units to the output unit of the network, $w_{hp}$. The precision vector is the vector of the weights of the precision readout described above, $w_{hψ}$. For the visualization, we orthogonalized the precision vector against the prediction vector using the Gram-Schmidt process (i.e. by subtracting from the precision vector its projection onto the prediction vector), and used the orthogonalized precision vector to define the y-axis shown in Figure 4b.

The perturbation experiment reported in Figure 5 is designed to test the causal role of the precision read from a given network on its weighting of the next observation, measured through its effective learning rate. We performed this perturbation experiment on each of the 20 networks that were trained within each of the four architectures we considered. The causal instrument is a perturbation vector q that is added to the network’s recurrent unit activations. The perturbation vector was randomly generated subject to the following constraints:

We describe below the algorithm that we used to generate random perturbations $q$ that satisfy these constraints. The idea is to decompose $q$ into two components: both components leave the prediction unaffected, the first ($q_{ψ}$) is used to induce a controlled change in precision, the second ($q_{r}$) does not change the precision but is added to ensure a constant intensity of the perturbation across simulations.

The experiment was run on a set of 1000 sample time points randomly drawn from 300 sequences. First, the unperturbed learning rate was measured by running the network on all of the sequences. Second, for each sample time point, the network was run unperturbed up until that point, a perturbation vector was randomly generated for the desired change of precision and applied to the network at that point, then the perturbed network was run on the next time point and its perturbed learning rate was measured. This was repeated for each level of change in precision. Finally, for a given change in precision, the change in learning rate was calculated as the difference between the perturbed and the unperturbed learning rate.

For statistical analysis, we ran a one-tailed paired t-test to test whether the population’s mean change in learning rate was higher at one level of precision change than at the next level of precision change. This was done for each of the four consecutive pairs of levels of change in precision.

### Test of higher-level inference about changes

For a given network architecture, higher-level inference about changes was assessed by comparing the population of 20 networks trained in the environment with coupled change points to the population of 20 networks trained in the environment with independent change points.

In Figure 7c, the change in unobserved bigram prediction for a given streak length m was computed as follows. First, prior sequences were generated and each network was run on each of the sequences. We generated initial sequences of 74 observations each with a probability of 0.2 for the 'observed' bigram (which will render its repetition surprising) and a probability p for the 'unobserved' bigram equal to 0.2 or 0.8 (such probabilities, symmetric and substantially different from the default prior 0.5, should render a change in their inferred value detectable). We crossed all possibilities (0|0 or 1|1 as observed bigram, 0.2 or 0.8 for p) and generated 100 sequences for each (hence 400 sequences total). Second, at the end of each of these initial sequences, the prediction for the unobserved bigram, pbefore, was queried by retrieving the output of the network after giving it as input ‘0’ if the unobserved bigram was 0|0 or ‘1’ otherwise. Third, the network was further presented with m repeated observations of the same value: ‘1’ if the observed bigram was 1|1 or ‘0’ otherwise. Finally, after this streak of repetition, the new prediction for the unobserved bigram, pafter, was queried (as before) and we measured its change with respect to the previous query, |pafter−pbefore|. This procedure was repeated for m ranging from 2 and 75.

For statistics, we ran a one-tailed two independent samples t-test to test whether the mean change in unobserved bigram prediction of the population trained on coupled change points was higher than that of the population trained on independent change points.

### Complexity analyses

The complexity analysis reported in Figure 8 consisted in measuring, for each network architecture and each environment, the performance of optimally trained networks as a function of the number of units N. For optimal training, hyperparameter optimization was repeated at several values of N, for each type of network and each environment (the resulting values are listed in Table 1). For the complexity analysis, a grid of equally spaced N values in logarithmic space between 1 and 45 was generated, an additional value of 474 was included specifically for the networks without recurrent weight training so as to match their number of trained parameters to that of an 11-unit gated recurrent network, and an additional value of 1,000 was included specifically for the networks without gating to facilitate the extrapolation. For every value on this grid, 20 networks of a given architecture in a given environment were randomly initialized with the set of hyperparameter values that was determined to be optimal for the nearest neighboring N value in logarithmic space. The performance of these networks after training was evaluated using a new couple of training and test datasets per environment, each consisting of 400 minibatches of 20 sequences for training and 1000 sequences for testing.

### Statistics

To assess the variability between different agent solutions, we trained 20 agents for each type of agent and each environment. These agents have different random seeds (which changes their parameter initialization and how their training data is shuffled). Throughout the article, we report mean or median over these agents, and individual data points when possible or 95 % confidence intervals (abbreviated as "CI") otherwise, as fully described in the text and figure legends. No statistical methods were used to pre-determine sample sizes but our sample sizes are similar to those reported in previous publications (Masse et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2019). Data analysis was not performed blind to the conditions of the experiments. No data were excluded from the analyses. All statistical tests were two-tailed unless otherwise noted. The data distribution was assumed to be normal, but this was not formally tested. The specific details of each statistical analysis are reported directly in the text.

There is no serious and quantitative comparison to behavior or neural data recorded in humans or animal models. All the comparisons are with other algorithms and reduced GRU networks. One can appreciate these comparisons if the goal is to show that a full GRU network is close to optimal (which, in many cases, it is). But do humans exhibit a similar level of optimality? One possibility would have been to provide some sort of analysis that would show that the types of errors the model makes are in some counterintuitive (or even intuitive) way like the types of errors humans make. In some of the papers where certain heuristics were proposed, the entire goal was to explain characteristic sub-optimalities in human behavior. As an example, see the recent paper from the Koechlin group in Nature Human Behavior. More generally, there is no shortage of papers quantifying human behavior in stochastic volatile environments. It would be great to see that the errors humans make in at least some task map onto the errors GRU networks make. Imagine for example that such a comparison would show that human errors are more similar to a lesioned version of the GRU, even though the full GRU is closer to optimal. The natural conclusion for such an observation would be that some of the proposed mechanisms are in fact not at play. In any case, all the reviewers think the comparison to human behavior would be valuable, and should be at minimum extensively discussed.

2. On the importance of gating: a lot of emphasis is put on the necessity of gating (eg title, abstract, discussion line 478). But the methods used in the paper cannot demonstrate necessity. Indeed other studies (see eg Collins, Sohl-Dickenstein and Sussillo, arxiv 2016) have argued that gating in RNNs improves their trainability, but does not increase their capacity. That study argued that large vanilla RNNs are able to reach the same performance as gated RNNs with more extensive training and/or hyper-parameter tuning. The claims and discussion should be revised to reflect this limitation.

3. The biological relevance of gating seems also somewhat over-stated (eg in the abstract): while there is no doubt various forms of gating are present in the nervous system, how they map to the specific time-dependent form used in GRUs is far from clear. The relationship of these gate variables with actual synapses, neurons, or populations of neurons is at best speculative at this point.

4. In terms of comparing to biology, the discussion states that "mapping between artificial units and biological neurons may not be straightforward." But biological and artificial models can still be compared quite effectively in terms of activity in the state space, and these comparisons can help reject hypotheses quite effectively. Training RNNs have been a productive avenue for understanding neural computations in the past years, in many studies of this class networks are constrained or contrasted by experimental data (Mante and Sussillo et al., 2013, Rajan et al., 2016 or Finkelstein and Fontolan et al., 2021 as some examples). It could have been possible to try to understand the geometry of neural representations of latent variables in network dynamics and how it is learned and depends on the environment. Additionally, by performing dynamical system analysis (see eg Susillo and Barak, 2013 or Dubreuil and Valente et al., bioRxiv as examples) it might be possible to understand the role of gating in the network computations.

5. The focus on very small network does not necessarily seem relevant when comparing with biologic networks (the phrase "reasonably sized networks" on l.479 seems inappropriate). The analysis of network size in Figure 7 goes until 45 units, which remains very small, and it's difficult to extrapolate the results to larger networks. For instance, large vanilla RNNs implement an effective form of gating based on their non=linearity (Dubreuil et al. 2020), and this mechanism may be able to drastically increase sequence-prediction performance.

6. Another weakness of the paper is that, for each new task, it trains a new GRU. Humans seem to be able to adapt to changes in the latent structure of the generative process without massive retraining. How does this flexibility map onto the proposed scheme? In one of the supplements, cross-task performances have been shown. One notable result is that a GRU trained on a changing bigram with or without coupled change points does quite poorly on the changing unigram. This is an example of failed generalization from a much more complex latent structure to a simpler one, which is indicative of overfitting (to the structure of a generative model – not its parameters). Somewhat counterintuitively, for the GRU model (as well as various other models), the smallest hit on generalization performance occurs when the models are trained on the changing unigram, which is the simplest latent structure considered. This is consistent with several psychophysical studies suggesting that humans may not rely on accurate latent models and may instead rely on simpler heuristics. In the end, is it justified to train new GRUs for each task?

7. Note that LSTMs are able to perform similar computations like the ones in this study here as is shown in Wang and Kurt-Nelson et al., 2019.

8. As a more technical point, the comparison with networks without gating does not seem fully fair. Freezing gating effectively reduces the number of time-dependent variables by a factor 3. Also, when freezing gating, one could treat the gating parameters as fixed hyper-parameters to be optimized, rather than setting them by hand to one.

claims.claim: For a given prediction error, the lower the precision, the higher the subsequent effective learning rate according to the precision-weighting principle.
claims.source: for a given prediction error, the lower the precision, the higher the subsequent effective learning rate.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the precision-weighting principle derived from probability theory.

claims.claim: Precision-weighting results in an automatic adjustment of the effective learning rate in response to a change, because the precision of the prediction decreases when a change is suspected.
claims.source: This precision-weighting principle results in an automatic adjustment of the effective learning rate in response to a change, because the precision of the prediction decreases when a change is suspected.
claims.evidence: This is an inference about the consequences of the precision-weighting principle.

claims.claim: Human participants can estimate not only the prediction but also its precision as estimated by the optimal agent.
claims.source: In line with this principle, human participants can estimate not only the prediction but also its precision as estimated by the optimal agent (Boldt et al., 2019, Figure 2; Meyniel et al., 2015, Figure 4B)
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior human studies.

claims.claim: In humans, precision relates to the participants' effective learning rate.
claims.source: and this precision indeed relates to the participants' effective learning rate (McGuire et al., 2014, Figure 2C and S1A; Nassar et al., 2010, Figure 4C and 3B; Nassar et al., 2012, Figure 5 and 7c, ).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior human studies.

claims.claim: The networks were trained only to maximize prediction accuracy, not to estimate precision.
claims.source: Note that the networks were trained only to maximize prediction accuracy (not to estimate precision).
claims.evidence: This is a description of the training procedure.

claims.claim: In gated recurrent networks, the read precision on left-out data was highly accurate, with a median Pearson correlation with the optimal precision of 0.82.
claims.source: Yet, in gated recurrent networks, we found that the read precision on left-out data was highly accurate (Figure 4a, left plot: the median Pearson correlation with the optimal precision is 0.82)
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by data shown in Figure 4a.

claims.claim: In gated recurrent networks, the read precision correlated with their subsequent effective learning rate with a median correlation of –0.79.
claims.source: and correlated with their subsequent effective learning rate as in the optimal agent (Figure 4a, right plot: the median correlation for gated recurrent networks is –0.79; for comparison, it is –0.88 for the optimal agent).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by data shown in Figure 4a.

claims.claim: In the optimal agent, the correlation between precision and subsequent effective learning rate is –0.88.
claims.source: for comparison, it is –0.88 for the optimal agent
claims.evidence: This is a measurement from the optimal agent for comparison.

claims.claim: In the gated recurrent network, the trajectories in the prediction-precision subspace are well separated along the precision axis, meaning that the representation of precision is not reducible to the prediction.
claims.source: First, in the gated recurrent network (Figure 4b, second plot from the right), the trajectories are well separated along the precision axis (for the same prediction, the network can represent multiple precisions), meaning that the representation of precision is not reducible to the prediction.
claims.evidence: This is a finding of the study, supported by visualization in Figure 4b.

claims.claim: In the network without gating, the trajectories in the prediction-precision subspace highly overlap, indicating that the representation of precision and prediction are mutually dependent.
claims.source: By contrast, in the network without gating (Figure 4b, rightmost plot), these trajectories highly overlap, which indicates that the representation of precision and prediction are mutually dependent.
claims.evidence: This is a finding of the study, supported by visualization in Figure 4b.

claims.claim: The mutual information between the read precision and the prediction of the network is very high in the network without gating (median MI = 5.2) compared to the gated recurrent network (median MI = 0.7) and the optimal agent (median MI = 0.6).
claims.source: To measure this dependence, we computed the mutual information between the read precision and the prediction of the network, and it turned out to be very high in the network without gating (median MI = 5.2) compared to the gated recurrent network (median MI = 0.7) and the optimal agent (median MI = 0.6) (without lateral connections, median MI = 1.3; without recurrent weight training, median MI = 1.9)
claims.evidence: This is a finding of the study, quantifying the dependence between precision and prediction.

claims.claim: In the gated recurrent network, the precision interacts dynamically with the prediction in a manner consistent with the precision-weighting principle: for a given prediction, the lower the precision, the larger the subsequent updates to the prediction.
claims.source: Second, in the gated recurrent network, the precision interacts dynamically with the prediction in a manner consistent with the precision-weighting principle: for a given prediction, the lower the precision, the larger the subsequent updates to the prediction (Figure 4b, vertical dotted line indicates the level of prediction and arrows the subsequent updates).
claims.evidence: This is a finding of the study, supported by visualization in Figure 4b.

claims.claim: In the network without gating, precision is confounded with prediction and the correlation between precision and effective learning rate is spuriously driven by the prediction itself.
claims.source: These results indicate that in the network without gating, precision is confounded with prediction and the correlation between precision and effective learning rate is spuriously driven by the prediction itself
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data about the network without gating.

claims.claim: In the network with gating, there is a genuine representation of precision beyond the prediction itself, which interacts with the updating of predictions.
claims.source: whereas in the network with gating, there is a genuine representation of precision beyond the prediction itself, which interacts with the updating of predictions.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data about the gated recurrent network.

claims.claim: Perturbations of the recurrent activity that induced a controlled change in the read precision caused significant changes in the networks' subsequent effective learning rate, commensurate with the induced change in precision.
claims.source: These perturbations caused significant changes in the networks' subsequent effective learning rate, commensurate with the induced change in precision, as predicted by the principle of precision-weighting (Figure 5, middle plot).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study from a causal perturbation experiment, supported by data shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: The causal relationship between precision and effective learning rate was abolished in the alternative networks that lacked one of the mechanisms of the gated recurrent architecture.
claims.source: Importantly, this causal relationship was abolished in the alternative networks that lacked one of the mechanisms of the gated recurrent architecture (Figure 5, right three plots; the slope of the effect was significantly different between the gated recurrent network group and any of the alternative network groups, two-tailed two independent samples t-test, all t(38) > 4.1, all p < 0.001, all Cohen's d > 1.3).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study from a causal perturbation experiment, supported by data shown in Figure 5 and statistical tests.

claims.claim: The gated recurrent networks' ability to adapt to changes relies on their precision-dependent updating.
claims.source: These results show that the gated recurrent networks' ability to adapt to changes indeed relies on their precision-dependent updating
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the causal perturbation experiment.

claims.claim: Precision-weighting does not arise without all three mechanisms of the gated recurrence.
claims.source: and that such precision-weighting does not arise without all three mechanisms of the gated recurrence.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the causal perturbation experiment.

claims.claim: In the changing bigram environment, the sequence of observations is generated according to two bigram probabilities p(0|0) and p(1|1).
claims.source: To study the ability to leverage such structure, we designed a new stochastic and changing environment in which the sequence of observations is no longer generated according to a single unigram probability, p(1), but two 'bigram probabilities' (also known as transition probabilities), p(0|0) and p(1|1), which denote the probability of occurrence of a 0 after a 0 and of a 1 after a 1, respectively (Figure 6a; see Figure 1—figure supplement 1 for a graphical model).
claims.evidence: This is a description of the changing bigram environment used in the study.

claims.claim: In the changing bigram environment, the bigram probabilities are changing randomly, with independent change points.
claims.source: These bigram probabilities are also changing randomly, with independent change points.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the changing bigram environment used in the study.

claims.claim: There is ample evidence that bigram probabilities play a key role in sequence knowledge in humans and other animals.
claims.source: This 'changing bigram environment' is well motivated because there is ample evidence that bigram probabilities play a key role in sequence knowledge in humans and other animals (Dehaene et al., 2015) even in the face of changes (Bornstein and Daw, 2013; Meyniel et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claims.claim: The gated recurrent networks achieved 98% of optimal prediction performance in the changing bigram environment.
claims.source: The gated recurrent networks achieved 98 % of optimal prediction performance (CI ±0.3%), outperforming the heuristic agents estimating bigram probabilities, and even more so those estimating a unigram probability (Figure 6c).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by data shown in Figure 6c.

claims.claim: Gated recurrent networks trained in the changing unigram environment performed much worse in the changing bigram environment.
claims.source: To demonstrate that this was due to their internalization of the latent structure, we also tested the gated recurrent networks that had been trained in the changing unigram environment: their performance was much worse (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is a finding of the study, supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: All three mechanisms of the gated recurrence are important for the ability to leverage the latent bigram structure.
claims.source: At the mechanistic level, all three mechanisms of the gated recurrence are important for this ability to leverage the latent bigram structure. Not only does the performance drop when one of these mechanisms is removed (Figure 6c)
claims.evidence: This is a finding of the study, supported by data shown in Figure 6c.

claims.claim: The drop in performance when one mechanism is removed is much larger in the bigram environment than in the unigram environment.
claims.source: but also this drop in performance is much larger than that observed in the changing unigram environment (without gating: –11.2 % [CI ±1.5 % calculated by Welch's t-interval] in the bigram environment vs. –5.5 % [CI ±0.6%] in the unigram environment, without lateral connections: –18.5 % [CI ±1.8%] vs. –2.9 % [CI ±0.2%]; without recurrent weight training: –29.9 % [CI ±1.6%] vs. –11.0 % [CI ±2.1%]; for every mechanism, there was a significant interaction effect between the removal of the mechanism and the environment on performance, all F(1,76) > 47.9, all p < 0.001).
claims.evidence: This is a finding of the study, supported by statistical tests.

claims.claim: Gated recurrent networks correctly incorporate the bigram context into predictions, changing predictions from one observation to the next according to the preceding observation as the optimal agent does.
claims.source: Figure 6b illustrates the gated recurrent networks' ability to correctly incorporate the bigram context into its predictions compared to networks lacking one of the mechanisms of the gated recurrence. While a gated recurrent network aptly changes its prediction from one observation to the next according to the preceding observation as the optimal agent does, the other networks fail to show such context-dependent behavior, sometimes even changing their prediction away from the optimal agent.
claims.evidence: This is a finding of the study, illustrated in Figure 6b.

claims.claim: Gated recurrent networks can leverage the latent bigram structure, but this ability is impaired when one mechanism of the gated recurrence is missing.
claims.source: Altogether these results show that gated recurrent networks can leverage the latent bigram structure, but this ability is impaired when one mechanism of the gated recurrence is missing.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data presented in Figure 6.

claims.claim: The read estimates of each of the latent bigram probabilities from gated recurrent network activity on left-out data were highly accurate, with Pearson correlation with the optimal estimates of 0.97 for each of the two bigram probabilities.
claims.source: We tested the latter possibility by trying to linearly read out the optimal estimate of each of the latent bigram probabilities from the recurrent activity of a gated recurrent network (see Materials and methods). Arguing in favor of an explicit representation, we found that the read estimates of each of the latent bigram probabilities on left-out data were highly accurate (Pearson correlation with the optimal estimates, median and CI: 0.97 [0.97, 0.98] for each of the two bigram probabilities).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study from readout analyses.

claims.claim: The read precisions of each bigram probability estimate from gated recurrent network activity on left-out data were quite accurate, with Pearson correlation with the optimal precisions of 0.77 for one bigram probability and 0.76 for the other.
claims.source: Again, we assessed the possibility to linearly read out the optimal precision of each estimate and found that the read precisions on left-out data were quite accurate (Pearson correlation with the optimal precisions, median and CI: 0.77 [0.74, 0.78] for one bigram probability and 0.76 [0.74, 0.78] for the other probability).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study from readout analyses.

claims.claim: The network successfully disentangles one bigram probability from the other since the read estimates can evolve independently from each other.
claims.source: Furthermore, it shows that the network successfully disentangles one bigram probability from the other since the read estimates can evolve independently from each other (for instance during the first 20 time steps, the value for 1|1 changes while the value for 0|0 does not, since only 1 s are observed).
claims.evidence: This is a finding of the study, illustrated in Figure 6d.

claims.claim: Both bigram probabilities are simultaneously represented in gated recurrent networks, even though only one of the two is needed at any one time for the prediction.
claims.source: It is particularly interesting that both bigram probabilities are simultaneously represented, given that only one of them is relevant for the moment-by-moment prediction read by the network's output unit (whose weights cannot change during the sequence).
claims.evidence: This is a finding of the study, illustrated in Figure 6d.

claims.claim: Gated recurrent networks internalize the latent bigram structure in such a way that both bigram probabilities are available simultaneously.
claims.source: We conclude that gated recurrent networks internalize the latent bigram structure in such a way that both bigram probabilities are available simultaneously, even though only one of the two is needed at any one time for the prediction.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the readout analyses.

claims.claim: In the changing bigram environment with coupled change points, the change points of the two bigram probabilities are coupled rather than independent.
claims.source: To study the ability to leverage such a hierarchical structure, we designed a third environment in which, in addition to bigram probabilities, we introduced a higher-level factor: the change points of the two bigram probabilities are now coupled, rather than independent as they were in the previous environment (Figure 7a; Figure 1—figure supplement 1 shows the hierarchical structure).
claims.evidence: This is a description of the environment used in the study.

claims.claim: Due to the coupling of change points, optimal prediction requires the ability to make a higher-level inference: having observed that the frequency of one of the bigrams has changed, one should transfer this suspicion of a change to the latent probability of the other bigram.
claims.source: Due to this coupling, from the agent's point of view, the likelihood that a change point has occurred depends on the observations about both bigrams. Thus, optimal prediction requires the ability to make a higher-level inference: having observed that the frequency of one of the bigrams has changed, one should not only suspect that the latent probability of this bigram has changed but also transfer this suspicion of a change to the latent probability of the other bigram, even without any observations about that bigram.
claims.evidence: This is an inference about the computational requirement for optimal prediction in this environment.

claims.claim: Such a transfer of suspicion of change has been reported in humans.
claims.source: Such a transfer has been reported in humans (Heilbron and Meyniel, 2019, Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a prior human study.

claims.claim: Gated recurrent networks trained in the coupled environment changed their prediction about the unobserved bigram significantly more than networks trained in the independent environment, across a large range of streak lengths.
claims.source: We found that gated recurrent networks trained in the coupled environment changed their prediction about the unobserved bigram significantly more than networks trained in the independent environment, and this was true across a large range of streak lengths (Figure 7c, top plot).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by data shown in Figure 7c.

claims.claim: The coupling of change points makes very little difference in terms of raw performance.
claims.source: The mere presence of this effect is particularly impressive given that the coupling makes very little difference in terms of raw performance (Figure 6—figure supplement 1, the networks trained in either the coupled or the independent environment perform very similarly when tested in either environment).
claims.evidence: This is a finding of the study, supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: All mechanisms of the gated recurrence are important to achieve higher-level inference since the networks deprived of either gating, lateral connections, or recurrent weight training did not show any effect of training environment on change in prediction.
claims.source: All mechanisms of the gated recurrence are important to achieve this higher-level inference since the networks deprived of either gating, lateral connections, or recurrent weight training did not show any effect, no matter the streak length (Figure 7c, bottom three plots; for every mechanism, there was a significant interaction effect between the removal of the mechanism and the training environment on the change in prediction over networks and streak lengths, all F(1,6076) > 43.2, all p < 0.001).
claims.evidence: This is a finding of the study, supported by data shown in Figure 7c and statistical tests.

claims.claim: Gated recurrent networks but not alternative networks leverage the higher level of structure where the change points of the latent probabilities are coupled.
claims.source: These results show that gated recurrent networks but not alternative networks leverage the higher level of structure where the change points of the latent probabilities are coupled.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data presented in Figure 7.

claims.claim: Gated recurrent networks can reach similar performance with even fewer than 11 units, especially in simpler environments.
claims.source: It turns out that gated recurrent networks can reach a similar performance with even fewer units, especially in simpler environments (Figure 8a and b, left plot).
claims.evidence: This is a finding of the study, supported by data shown in Figure 8.

claims.claim: In the unigram environment, gated recurrent networks reach 99% of their asymptotic performance with no more than 3 units.
claims.source: For instance, in the unigram environment, gated recurrent networks reach 99 % of their asymptotic performance with no more than 3 units.
claims.evidence: This is a finding of the study, supported by data shown in Figure 8.

claims.claim: Without either gating, lateral connections, or recurrent weight training, even when the networks are provided with more units to match the number of trained parameters in the 11-unit gated recurrent networks, they are unable to achieve similar performance.
claims.source: By contrast, without either gating, lateral connections, or recurrent weight training, even when the networks are provided with more units to match the number of trained parameters in the 11-unit gated recurrent networks, they are unable to achieve similar performance (Figure 8a and b, right three plots, the twin x-axes indicate the number of units and trained parameters).
claims.evidence: This is a finding of the study, supported by data shown in Figure 8.

claims.claim: With an unlimited number of units, vanilla RNNs will be able to achieve similar performance to gated recurrent networks since they are universal approximators of dynamical systems.
claims.source: With an unlimited number of units, at least in the case without gating (i.e. a vanilla RNN, short for recurrent neural network), the networks will be able to achieve such performance since they are universal approximators of dynamical systems (Cybenko, 1989; Schäfer and Zimmermann, 2006).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior theoretical work on universal approximation.

claims.claim: The slow growth of the vanilla RNNs' performance with the number of units is well described by a power law function.
claims.source: Indeed, the slow growth of the vanilla RNNs' performance with the number of units is well described by a power law function, of the form: (100−p) = c(1/N)α, where p is the % of optimal performance and N is the number of units.
claims.evidence: This is a finding of the study from fitting the performance data.

claims.claim: The power law fitted in the unigram environment using the obtained performance from 2 to 45 units yielded a goodness-of-fit of R2 = 92.4%.
claims.source: We fitted this law in the unigram environment using the obtained performance from 2 to 45 units and it yielded a goodness-of-fit of R2 = 92.4% (fitting was done by linear regression on the logarithm of N and (100−p)).
claims.evidence: This is a finding of the study from fitting the performance data.

claims.claim: The power law predicted performance at 1,000 units was within 0.2% of the obtained performance for vanilla RNNs of this size.
claims.source: To further confirm the validity of the power law, we then extrapolated to 1,000 units and found that the predicted performance was within 0.2 % of the obtained performance for networks of this size (predicted: 97.8%, obtained: 97.6%).
claims.evidence: This is a finding of the study validating the power law extrapolation.

claims.claim: Based on the power law, more than 10^4 units would be needed for the vanilla RNN to reach the performance exhibited by the GRU with only 11 units.
claims.source: Based on this power law, more than 104 units would be needed for the vanilla RNN to reach the performance exhibited by the GRU with only 11 units.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the fitted power law.

claims.claim: The number of units is a fair measure of space complexity across the architectures considered, since in all of them it is equal to the number of state variables.
claims.source: Note that, in terms of computational complexity, the number of units is a fair measure of space complexity (i.e. the amount of memory) across the architectures we considered, since in all of them it is equal to the number of state variables (having one state variable hi per unit, see Materials and methods).
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the measure of complexity used in the study.

claims.claim: It is the specific computational properties provided by the combination of the three mechanisms that afford effective low-complexity solutions.
claims.source: Therefore, it is the specific computational properties provided by the combination of the three mechanisms that afford effective low-complexity solutions.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the complexity analyses.

claims.claim: Gated recurrent networks perform quasi-optimally in environments fraught with randomness, changes, and different levels of latent structure with only 11 units.
claims.source: We have shown that the gated recurrent architecture enables simple and effective solutions: with only 11 units, the networks perform quasi-optimally in environments fraught with randomness, changes, and different levels of latent structure.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the main findings of the study.

claims.claim: Gated recurrent network solutions reproduce several aspects of optimality observed in organisms, including the adaptation of their effective learning rate, the ability to represent the precision of their estimation and to use it to weight their updates, and the ability to represent and leverage the latent structure of the environment.
claims.source: Moreover, these solutions reproduce several aspects of optimality observed in organisms, including the adaptation of their effective learning rate, the ability to represent the precision of their estimation and to use it to weight their updates, and the ability to represent and leverage the latent structure of the environment.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the main findings of the study.

claims.claim: Three mechanisms are important to achieve gated recurrent network solutions: gating, lateral connections, and the training of recurrent weights.
claims.source: By depriving the architecture of one of its mechanisms, we have shown that three of them are important to achieve such solutions: gating, lateral connections, and the training of recurrent weights.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the main findings of the study.

claims.claim: From a computational viewpoint, there exists no tractable solution (even approximate) for Bayesian inference in an arbitrary environment, since it is NP-hard.
claims.source: From a computational viewpoint, there exists no tractable solution (even approximate) for Bayesian inference in an arbitrary environment, since it is NP-hard (Cooper, 1990; Dagum and Luby, 1993).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work on computational complexity.

claims.claim: Being a bounded agent, the brain cannot solve Bayesian inference in its most general form.
claims.source: Being a bounded agent (Simon, 1955; Simon, 1972), the brain cannot solve Bayesian inference in its most general form.
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations and draws from established knowledge about bounded rationality.

claims.claim: The study provides an existence proof that there exist plausible solutions that are almost indistinguishable from Bayesian inference in the changing unigram and changing bigram environments.
claims.source: In the changing unigram and changing bigram environments, our results provide an existence proof: there exist plausible solutions that are almost indistinguishable from Bayesian inference (i.e. the optimal solution).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the findings of the study.

claims.claim: The gated recurrent network solutions exhibit qualitative properties of Bayesian inference that have been demonstrated in humans but are lacking in heuristic solutions.
claims.source: They exhibit qualitative properties of Bayesian inference that have been demonstrated in humans but are lacking in heuristic solutions, such as the dynamic adjustment of the effective learning rate (Behrens et al., 2007; Nassar et al., 2010; Nassar et al., 2012), the internal representation of latent variables and the precision of their estimates (Boldt et al., 2019; Meyniel et al., 2015), the precision-weighting of updates (McGuire et al., 2014; Nassar et al., 2010; Nassar et al., 2012), and the ability for higher-level inference (Bill et al., 2020; Heilbron and Meyniel, 2019; Purcell and Kiani, 2016).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior human studies and draws from the findings of the current study.

claims.claim: The performance obtained with the gated recurrent architecture is consistent with the numerous other successes it produced in other cognitive neuroscience tasks.
claims.source: The performance we obtained with the gated recurrent architecture is consistent with the numerous other successes it produced in other cognitive neuroscience tasks (Wang et al., 2018; Yang et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claims.claim: The gated recurrent architecture offers quasi-optimal low-complexity solutions to new and difficult challenges, including those posed by bigram and higher-level structures and latent probabilities that change unpredictably anywhere in the unit interval.
claims.source: Our detailed study reveals that it offers quasi-optimal low-complexity solutions to new and difficult challenges, including those posed by bigram and higher-level structures and latent probabilities that change unpredictably anywhere in the unit interval.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the findings of the study.

claims.claim: The mechanisms of gated recurrence do not include any components specifically designed to perform certain probabilistic operations or estimate certain types of latent variables.
claims.source: One of the advantages of such mechanisms is their generic character: they do not include any components specifically designed to perform certain probabilistic operations or estimate certain types of latent variables, as often done in neuroscience (Echeveste et al., 2020; Fusi et al., 2007; Jazayeri and Movshon, 2006; Ma et al., 2006; Pecevski et al., 2011; Soltani and Wang, 2010).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations and draws from the design of the mechanisms.

claims.claim: The mechanisms of gated recurrence allow adaptive behavior only through recurrent activity dynamics, without involving synaptic plasticity.
claims.source: In addition, they allow adaptive behavior only through recurrent activity dynamics, without involving synaptic plasticity as in other models (Farashahi et al., 2017; Fusi et al., 2005; Iigaya, 2016; Schultz et al., 1997).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations and draws from the design of the mechanisms.

claims.claim: Recurrent dynamics allow the networks to quickly adapt to a given change in the environment.
claims.source: Our study supports this view: recurrent dynamics allow the networks to quickly adapt to a given change in the environment (Figure 3)
claims.evidence: This is a finding of the study, supported by data shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: Synaptic plasticity allows the training process to tune the speed of adaptation to the frequency of change of the environment.
claims.source: while synaptic plasticity allows the training process to tune the speed of this adaptation to the frequency of change of the environment (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is a finding of the study, supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Without one of the three mechanisms (gating, lateral connections, or recurrent weight training), a very large number of units would be needed to achieve comparable performance to gated recurrent networks.
claims.source: Our findings suggest that these mechanisms are particularly advantageous to enable solutions with low computational complexity. Without one of them, it seems that a very large number of units (i.e. a large amount of memory) would be needed to achieve comparable performance (Figure 8)
claims.evidence: This is a finding of the study, supported by data shown in Figure 8.

claims.claim: The three mechanisms seem to be key computational building blocks to build simple and effective solutions.
claims.source: These mechanisms thus seem to be key computational building blocks to build simple and effective solutions.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the findings of the study.

claims.claim: The brain has limited computational resources, often quantified by the Shannon capacity.
claims.source: and it is important for the brain since the brain has limited computational resources (often quantified by the Shannon capacity, i.e. the number of bits that can be transmitted per unit of time, which here amounts to the number of units) (Bhui et al., 2021; Lieder and Griffiths, 2019).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations and draws from established knowledge about brain constraints.

claims.claim: Simplicity promotes understanding.
claims.source: Moreover, simplicity promotes our understanding, and it is with the same goal of understanding that others have used model reduction in large networks (Dubreuil et al., 2020; Jazayeri and Ostojic, 2021; Schaeffer et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations and draws from established methodological principles.

claims.claim: Extensive hyperparameter optimization was conducted to maximize the chances that the best possible performance is achieved after training.
claims.source: However, to maximize the chances that the best possible performance is achieved after training, we conducted an extensive hyperparameter optimization, repeated for each environment, architecture, and several number of units, until there is no more improvement according to the Bayesian optimization (see Materials and methods).
claims.evidence: This is a description of the methodological approach.

claims.claim: Recurrent connections are ubiquitous in the brain.
claims.source: Recurrent connections are ubiquitous in the brain (Douglas and Martin, 2007; Hunt and Hayden, 2017)
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior neuroscience work.

claims.claim: Many forms of gating have been observed in neuroscience, and they can generally be grouped into three categories: neural circuits, neural oscillations, and neuromodulation.
claims.source: In neuroscience, many forms of gating have been observed, and they can generally be grouped into three categories according to the neural process that supports them: neural circuits, neural oscillations, and neuromodulation.
claims.evidence: This is a general statement about neuroscience findings, drawing from established knowledge.

claims.claim: In neural circuits, a specific pathway can be gated through inhibition/disinhibition by inhibitory (GABAergic) neurons.
claims.source: In neural circuits, a specific pathway can be gated through inhibition/disinhibition by inhibitory (GABAergic) neurons. This has been observed in microscopic circuits, e.g. in pyramidal neurons a dendritic pathway can be gated by interneurons (Costa et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2016), or macroscopic circuits, for example in basal ganglia-thalamo-cortical circuits a cortico-cortical pathway can be gated by the basal ganglia and the mediodorsal nucleus of thalamus (O'Reilly, 2006; O'Reilly and Frank, 2006; Rikhye et al., 2018; Wang and Halassa, 2021; Yamakawa, 2020).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior neuroscience work.

claims.claim: An effective gating can be achieved by a large population of interacting neurons taking advantage of their nonlinearity.
claims.source: In addition to inhibition/disinhibition, an effective gating can also be achieved by a large population of interacting neurons taking advantage of their nonlinearity (Beiran et al., 2021; Dubreuil et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claims.claim: Experiments have shown that activity in certain frequency bands (typically, alpha and beta) can gate behavioral and neuronal responses to the same stimulus.
claims.source: Regarding neural oscillations, experiments have shown that activity in certain frequency bands (typically, alpha and beta) can gate behavioral and neuronal responses to the same stimulus (Baumgarten et al., 2016; Busch et al., 2009; Hipp et al., 2011; Iemi et al., 2019; Klimesch, 1999; Mathewson et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior neuroscience work.

claims.claim: The binding of certain neuromodulators to certain receptors of a synapse changes the gain of its input-output transfer function, thus changing its effective weight.
claims.source: Finally, the binding of certain neuromodulators to the certain receptors of a synapse changes the gain of its input-output transfer function, thus changing its effective weight. This has been demonstrated in neurophysiological studies implicating noradrenaline (Aston-Jones and Cohen, 2005; Salgado et al., 2016; Servan-Schreiber et al., 1990), dopamine (Moyer et al., 2007; Servan-Schreiber et al., 1990; Stalter et al., 2020; Thurley et al., 2008), and acetylcholine (Gil et al., 1997; Herrero et al., 2008) (see review in Thiele and Bellgrove, 2018).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior neuroscience work.

claims.claim: Gated recurrence provides plausible solutions for the brain because its mechanisms can all be biologically implemented and lead to efficient solutions.
claims.source: We claim that gated recurrence provides plausible solutions for the brain because its mechanisms can all be biologically implemented and lead to efficient solutions.
claims.evidence: This is a claim based on the findings of the study and knowledge about biological implementation.

claims.claim: Given the multiple biological realizability of gated recurrence mechanisms, the mapping between artificial units and biological neurons is not straightforward.
claims.source: However, given their multiple biological realizability, the mapping between artificial units and biological neurons is not straightforward: one unit may map to a large population of neurons (e.g. a brain area), or even to a microscopic, subneuronal component (e.g. the dendritic level).
claims.evidence: This is an inference about the relationship between the model and biology.

claims.claim: It is important to adjust the recurrent weights and thus the network dynamics to the environment.
claims.source: Regarding the training, our results highlight that it is important to adjust the recurrent weights and thus the network dynamics to the environment (and not fix them as in reservoir computing [Tanaka et al., 2019])
claims.evidence: This is a finding of the study, supported by comparisons with reservoir computing.

claims.claim: The biological process that leads to adjustment of recurrent weights could occur during development, the life span, or the evolution process.
claims.source: It could occur during development (Sherman et al., 2020), the life span (Lillicrap et al., 2020), or the evolution process (Zador, 2019) (these possibilities are not mutually exclusive).
claims.evidence: This is speculation about possible biological processes, supported by citations.

claims.claim: The training procedure relies only on the observation sequence, leveraging prediction error signals, which have been found in the brain in many studies.
claims.source: First, it relies only on the observation sequence (no supervision or reinforcement), leveraging prediction error signals, which have been found in the brain in many studies (den Ouden et al., 2012; Eshel et al., 2013; Maheu et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior neuroscience work.

claims.claim: In predictive coding, the computation of prediction errors is part of the prediction process.
claims.source: Importantly, in predictive coding (Rao and Ballard, 1999), the computation of prediction errors is part of the prediction process; here we are suggesting that it may also be part of the training process (as argued in O'Reilly et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations and draws from established theory.

claims.claim: Relatively few iterations of training suffice for the networks to reach high performance.
claims.source: Second, relatively few iterations of training suffice (Figure 8—figure supplement 1, in the order of 10–100; for comparison, Wang et al., 2018 reported training for 40,000 episodes in an environment similar to ours).
claims.evidence: This is a finding of the study, supported by data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1 and comparison to prior work.

claims.claim: In the laboratory, human behavior is often at best qualitatively Bayesian but quantitatively suboptimal.
claims.source: In the laboratory, their behavior is often at best qualitatively Bayesian but quantitatively suboptimal.
claims.evidence: This is a general statement about human behavior drawing from established knowledge.

claims.claim: Although humans adjust their effective learning rate to changes, the base value of their learning rate and their dynamic adjustments may depart from the optimal values.
claims.source: For example, although they adjust their effective learning rate to changes, the base value of their learning rate and their dynamic adjustments may depart from the optimal values (Nassar et al., 2010; Nassar et al., 2012; Prat-Carrabin et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior human studies.

claims.claim: Humans may not update their prediction on every trial, unlike the optimal solution.
claims.source: They may also not update their prediction on every trial, unlike the optimal solution (Gallistel et al., 2014; Khaw et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior human studies.

claims.claim: There is substantial interindividual variability in human behavior which does not exist in the optimal solution.
claims.source: Finally, there is substantial interindividual variability which does not exist in the optimal solution (Khaw et al., 2021; Nassar et al., 2010; Nassar et al., 2012; Prat-Carrabin et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior human studies.

claims.claim: If already trained gated recurrent networks exist in the brain, then one can be used in a new but similar enough environment without further training.
claims.source: If already trained gated recurrent networks exist in the brain, then one can be used in a new but similar enough environment without further training.
claims.evidence: This is a speculation about the implications of the findings.

claims.claim: In laboratory experiments, humans perform reasonably well with almost no training but explicit task instructions given in natural language, along with a baggage of prior experience.
claims.source: This is an interesting possibility because, in laboratory experiments mirroring our study, humans perform reasonably well with almost no training but explicit task instructions given in natural language, along with a baggage of prior experience (Gallistel et al., 2014; Heilbron and Meyniel, 2019; Khaw et al., 2021; Meyniel et al., 2015; Peterson and Beach, 1967).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior human studies.

claims.claim: A gated recurrent network can still perform well in conditions different from those it was trained in: across probabilities of change points and latent structures.
claims.source: In favor of the possibility to reuse an existing solution, we found that a gated recurrent network can still perform well in conditions different from those it was trained in: across probabilities of change points (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) and latent structures (Figure 6—figure supplement 1, from bigram to unigram).
claims.evidence: This is a finding of the study, supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: In a gated recurrent network, the representations of latent probabilities and the precision of these probability estimates are linearly readable from recurrent activity.
claims.source: One of our findings may be particularly interesting to experimentalists: in a gated recurrent network, the representations of latent probabilities and the precision of these probability estimates (sometimes referred to as confidence [Boldt et al., 2019; Meyniel et al., 2015], estimation uncertainty [McGuire et al., 2014; Payzan-LeNestour et al., 2013], or epistemic uncertainty [Amini et al., 2020; Friston et al., 2015; Pezzulo et al., 2015]) are linearly readable from recurrent activity, the form of decoding most frequently used in neuroscience (Haxby et al., 2014; Kriegeskorte and Diedrichsen, 2019).
claims.evidence: This is a finding of the study, supported by citations to prior work on decoding methods.

claims.claim: The representations of latent probabilities and precision arise spontaneously in gated recurrent networks, and their emergence seems to come from the computational properties of gated recurrence together with the need to perform well in a stochastic and changing environment.
claims.source: These representations arise spontaneously, and their emergence seems to come from the computational properties of gated recurrence together with the need to perform well in a stochastic and changing environment.
claims.evidence: This is an inference about the origin of the representations based on the findings.

claims.claim: If gated recurrent networks can be found in the brain, then latent probability estimates and their precision should be decodable in brain signals.
claims.source: This yields an empirical prediction: if such networks can be found in the brain, then latent probability estimates and their precision should also be decodable in brain signals, as already found in some studies (Bach et al., 2011; McGuire et al., 2014; Meyniel, 2020; Meyniel and Dehaene, 2017; Payzan-LeNestour et al., 2013; Tomov et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is a prediction based on the findings, supported by citations to prior neuroscience studies.

results.result: Gated recurrent networks with 11 units achieve quasi-optimal performance (99% of optimal) in the changing unigram environment, significantly outperforming heuristic agents and networks lacking any of the three key mechanisms (gating, lateral connections, or recurrent weight training).
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C69 provide quantitative performance data from Figure 2b showing the gated recurrent network achieves 99% optimal performance and systematically outperforms all alternatives. The statistical comparisons (p < 0.001) and confidence intervals support the conclusion that all three mechanisms are necessary. The sample size (n=20 per architecture) and methodological rigor are adequate.

results.result: Gated recurrent networks dynamically adjust their effective learning rate in response to change points, matching the optimal agent's behavior with characteristic peaks at the same time and amplitude, while heuristic agents and networks lacking key mechanisms fail to show this adaptation.
results.evaluation: Claims C73 and C76-C77 are supported by quantitative data in Figure 3b showing the gated recurrent network's effective learning rate closely matches the optimal agent, while alternative architectures show degraded performance. The analysis is based on 20 networks per architecture tested on 10,000 sequences with locked change points, providing adequate statistical power.

results.result: Gated recurrent networks spontaneously develop internal representations of precision that are linearly decodable from recurrent activity (median correlation 0.82 with optimal precision) and that interact dynamically with predictions according to the precision-weighting principle, with precision and prediction being separable representations (MI = 0.7) unlike in networks without gating (MI = 5.2).
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C86 and C88-C91 are supported by readout analyses on left-out data (Figure 4a-b) showing high correlation with optimal precision and proper separation from prediction. The mutual information analysis (C90) quantitatively demonstrates that gating enables independent representation of precision and prediction. The linear readout methodology is standard and appropriate.

results.result: Causal perturbation experiments demonstrate that the internal representation of precision causally regulates the effective learning rate in gated recurrent networks, with this causal relationship abolished in networks lacking any of the three key mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C95 are supported by the perturbation experiment (Figure 5) showing significant effects in gated recurrent networks (p < 0.001, Cohen's d > 1.3) that are abolished in alternative architectures. The experimental design properly controls for prediction error by keeping predictions constant while manipulating precision. The sample size (n=20 per architecture, 1000 sample time points) is adequate.

results.result: Gated recurrent networks achieve 98% optimal performance in the changing bigram environment and internalize the latent bigram structure, with both bigram probabilities simultaneously represented and linearly decodable (correlation 0.97 for estimates, 0.77 for precisions), while networks lacking any mechanism show larger performance drops than in the unigram environment.
results.evaluation: Claims C101-C111 are supported by performance data (Figure 6c) and readout analyses (Figure 6d) on left-out data. The interaction effects between mechanism removal and environment (all F(1,76) > 47.9, p < 0.001) demonstrate that all three mechanisms are more critical for bigram than unigram environments. The simultaneous representation of both bigram probabilities despite only one being needed at any time is a notable finding.

results.result: Gated recurrent networks trained in environments with coupled change points demonstrate higher-level inference by transferring suspicion of change from one bigram to another, an effect that requires all three mechanisms and occurs despite minimal impact on raw performance.
results.evaluation: Claims C115-C117 are supported by data in Figure 7c showing significant differences between networks trained on coupled vs. independent change points across streak lengths, with significant interaction effects (all F(1,6076) > 43.2, p < 0.001). The finding that this occurs despite minimal performance differences (C116, Figure 6—figure supplement 1) strengthens the conclusion that networks genuinely learn the hierarchical structure.

results.result: Gated recurrent networks achieve near-optimal performance with very few units (3 units for 99% performance in unigram environment), while alternative architectures require orders of magnitude more units, with vanilla RNNs following a power law requiring >10^4 units to match 11-unit gated recurrent network performance.
results.evaluation: Claims C119-C126 are supported by complexity analyses in Figure 8 showing performance as a function of network size. The power law fit (R² = 92.4%) and validation at 1000 units (predicted 97.8%, observed 97.6%) support the extrapolation to >10^4 units. However, the extrapolation to such large networks involves assumptions about continued power law behavior that cannot be directly verified.

results.result: The gated recurrent architecture with all three mechanisms (gating, lateral connections, recurrent weight training) enables simple and effective solutions that perform quasi-optimally and reproduce multiple aspects of optimal behavior observed in organisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C129-C131 are summary statements supported by the collective evidence from all prior results. The consistent finding across multiple environments and analyses that all three mechanisms are necessary provides strong support for this overarching conclusion.

results.result: The study provides an existence proof that plausible neural network solutions can be nearly indistinguishable from Bayesian inference in changing unigram and bigram environments, exhibiting qualitative properties demonstrated in humans but lacking in heuristic solutions.
results.evaluation: Claims C134-C135 are supported by the performance data showing 99% and 98% optimal performance in the two environments, along with demonstrations of precision representation, precision-weighting, and higher-level inference. The comparison to human behavior is supported by citations to prior studies (C82-C83, C114). This represents a valid existence proof within the tested environments.

results.result: The three mechanisms of gated recurrence are generic (not specifically designed for probabilistic operations), enable adaptation through recurrent dynamics without synaptic plasticity during task performance, and are key computational building blocks for low-complexity solutions.
results.evaluation: Claims C137-C143 are supported by the mechanistic analyses showing that the generic mechanisms enable quasi-optimal performance across different environments and that removing any mechanism dramatically increases the complexity required (Figure 8). The distinction between recurrent dynamics for rapid adaptation (C140, Figure 3) and synaptic plasticity for tuning to environment statistics (C141, Figure 3—figure supplement 1) is empirically supported.

results.result: The mechanisms of gated recurrence (gating, lateral connections, recurrent weight training) have multiple plausible biological implementations in the brain, including inhibition/disinhibition circuits, neural oscillations, and neuromodulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C147-C153 are supported by extensive citations to prior neuroscience work demonstrating various forms of gating and recurrent connections in the brain. However, this is primarily a review of existing literature rather than new empirical findings. The claim that these mechanisms provide plausible solutions (C153) is an inference combining the computational results with biological knowledge.

results.result: Training recurrent weights to the environment is important for performance, the training procedure uses only observation sequences with prediction error signals found in the brain, and relatively few training iterations (10-100) suffice for high performance.
results.evaluation: Claims C155 and C159 are supported by data showing that networks without recurrent weight training perform poorly (Figure 2b) and that training converges quickly (Figure 8—figure supplement 1). Claim C157 is supported by citations to prior work on prediction error signals in the brain. These are methodological findings that support the biological plausibility of the approach.

results.result: Gated recurrent networks can generalize across different change point probabilities and latent structures, and the spontaneous emergence of linearly decodable representations of latent probabilities and precision yields the empirical prediction that these should be decodable in brain signals.
results.evaluation: Claim C166 is supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1 showing cross-environment performance. Claims C167-C168 are supported by the readout analyses. Claim C169 is a valid prediction based on the findings, with supporting citations to some existing studies showing such decodability. This represents a testable prediction for future neuroscience experiments.

results.result: Human behavior in laboratory tasks is often qualitatively Bayesian but quantitatively suboptimal, with deviations including suboptimal learning rate adjustments, intermittent updating, and substantial interindividual variability.
results.evaluation: Claims C160-C163 are supported by citations to multiple prior human studies. This is a review of existing literature on human suboptimalities rather than new findings. The authors acknowledge these limitations and suggest future directions for modeling suboptimalities.

results.result: The methodological choices of using small networks (11 units), training 20 agents per architecture, and conducting extensive hyperparameter optimization ensure that the solutions are simple, statistically reliable, and near-optimal.
results.evaluation: Claims C38, C54-C56, C63, and C146 describe methodological choices that are well-justified and properly implemented. The choice of 11 units is empirically justified (C55), the sample size of 20 provides adequate statistical power, and the Bayesian hyperparameter optimization is thorough. These are sound methodological decisions.

results.result: The introduction establishes that prediction is crucial across cognitive domains, poses computational challenges in real-world environments (stochastic, changing, structured), and that while Bayesian inference is optimal it is computationally intractable, while heuristics lack generality and biological implementation remains unclear.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C36 are background statements supported by citations to prior work and established knowledge in the field. These provide appropriate context and motivation for the study but do not represent new empirical findings.

results.result: Bayesian inference in arbitrary environments is NP-hard and the brain as a bounded agent cannot solve it in its most general form.
results.evaluation: Claims C132-C133 are supported by citations to computational complexity theory (Cooper, 1990; Dagum and Luby, 1993) and bounded rationality (Simon, 1955; 1972). This is established knowledge that provides important context for interpreting the results.

results.result: The study uses a sequence prediction framework with three environments (changing unigram, changing bigram with independent change points, changing bigram with coupled change points) that are stochastic, changing, and feature increasing levels of latent structure, tested with network architectures following a common three-layer template with varying mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C59, C98-C99, and C112 describe the experimental framework, environments, and architectures. These are clearly defined and well-motivated by connections to prior experimental paradigms (C58, C100). The framework is appropriate for testing the research questions.

results.result: The discussion addresses the biological plausibility of the mechanisms, their ubiquity in the brain, implications for understanding brain function, and connections to human behavior, while acknowledging limitations and speculating about future directions.
results.evaluation: Claims C10-C11, C136, C144-C145, C154, C156, C158, C164-C165 mix established knowledge (C10, C144, C147), citations to prior work (C136, C165), inferences from the current findings (C154), and speculation about biological implementation and future work (C11, C156, C158, C164). While the discussion is thoughtful and well-grounded, many claims are speculative or represent interpretations rather than direct empirical findings.
